paper_title: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

sections.content: 1. Introduction Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both gripper and dexterous hand. Code & Website. World models built on joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict how scenes latent changes under an action and plan toward the latent of goal [4, 79, 110]. However, current JEPA world models have two significant challenges in robot manipulation, which hinges on metric 3D geometry: First, most JEPA world models read 2D input. Pointcloud JEPAs mostly pretrain encoders without actions [27, 36, 75, 115] or forecast LiDAR occupancy [112], so metric geometry rarely reaches the model that predicts and acts. An image entangles metric geometry with appearance and perspective, so pixel model must infer depth, whereas point cloud from the same camera records visible surfaces at their metric positions  (Fig. 3)  . Even web-scale 2D foundation features show limited 3D awareness [18]. LeWM [50], trained from pixels without pretraining, has its lowest success on OGBench Cube [61], where it trails DINOWM [110] on frozen DINOv2 features (74% vs. 86%) [50]. Its authors relate this gap partly to the 3D nature of the scene [50]. Second, what these models imagine stays hidden. JEPA latents are trained to be predictable, not reconstructive. Existing tools only decode them to images [50, 110] or audit them indirectly [50, 84], so the imagined 3D scene stays out of sight, which hampers debugging and real-robot safety checks. Scores do not reveal it either. JEPA world models are mostly scored in simulation by short-horizon goal reaching [50, 79, 110], where sampling-based planner such as the cross-entropy method [15] searches few action blocks for the predicted latent closest to goal latent. Such search tests the predictor over short, in-distribution horizons, not how well the latents serve the policies robots learn. For example, LeWM latents that plan well transfer poorly to policy learning [45], and the model is evaluated only in simulation [50]. Frozen-encoder imitation on established suites such as CortexBench [51] asks instead how well representation lets policy learn skill from few demonstrations, which matters when robot data are scarce. However, JEPA world models rarely face it. To address these two challenges, we propose JEPA4R, JEPA world model designed to see metric geometry and to show what it imagines, so that robots predictions can be checked before it acts. It reads single-camera point cloud through parameter-matched encoder  (Fig. 2)  . Every point cloud is paired with an image from the same eye-to-hand camera, so the 2D JEPAs are trained or evaluated on the same trajectories and viewpoint. To evaluate how JEPA4R performs in robot policy learning, we train policy head on the frozen latents under established protocols. Specifically, we use goal-conditioned policy learning on OGBench [61] and imitation on CortexBench, where JEPA4R is ranked among published representations and 2D JEPAs evaluated on the same data. JEPA4R predicts, plans and acts in the 4D point latent space of its encoder, and we call this 4D point planning. An imagined rollout is the latent sequence that the predictor generates autoregressively from context frames and actions. decoder attached to the frozen world model shows this imagination by turning every imagined rollout into decoded 4D rollout (Fig. 1a). All world models train in simulation. The RM75-B twin, digital twin of the RealMan RM75B arm, lets JEPA4Rs twin-trained world models and policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm. Notably, we evaluate policy learning on manipulation suites with colored point clouds from pipeline that also runs on the real arm, while previous work [58] evaluates planning alone with xyzonly raycast point clouds and finds the two modalities on par. JEPA4R leads the 2D JEPAs on OGBench Cube and Scene and ranks first on CortexBench, above every published representation (Tabs. 1 and 2, Fig. 4). Its decoder recovers the observed scene from encoded and predicted latents alike, so even long imagined rollouts stay close to the observed point clouds (Tab. 3, Fig. 7). On the real arm, JEPA4Rs twin-trained policies run with both parallel gripper and dexterous hand. In general, our paper can be summarized in the following three points: 4D point planning: we propose JEPA4R, which predicts, plans and acts in the latent space of realistic single-depthcamera point clouds, to bring the metric 3D geometry that 2D inputs leave implicit into JEPA world models. Latent-space reconstruction: we propose decoder attached to the frozen world model that turns every imagined rollout into 4D point clouds, to show what JEPA world models imagine, which their latents keep hidden. The decoded imagination keeps mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 environment steps, so it can be inspected for debugging and real-robot safety checks. Experiments on benchmarks and in the real world: we learn policies on OGBench and CortexBench in paired 2D/3D evaluation, where JEPA4Rs point-cloud features rank first on CortexBench, above every published representation and 2D JEPA. JEPA4R transfers zero-shot to the real arm with both gripper and dexterous hand, after training only in digital twin. 2. Related work JEPA and latent world models. JEPA world models extend joint-embedding prediction [3, 5, 8, 20, 53, 54, 91] to action-conditioned dynamics and regress latents, unlike world models that generate observations [7, 22] or predict rewards [24]. DINO-WM [110] and V-JEPA 2-AC [4] learn predictors on frozen foundation features, whereas PLDM [79] and LeWM [50] train encoder and predictor end to end. Follow-up work analyzes planning success [2, 81], generalization beyond expert rollouts [57], counterfactual action evaluation [80] and behavioral monitoring [84], and adds objectives for action sensitivity, physical-state grounding [96, 104, 106], object-level masking [56] and policy transfer [45], but all these models observe images, whose features show limited 3D awareness [18]. JEPA world models are mostly scored by planning success [49, 50, 79, 110], and PSG-JEPA [96] adds policy learning, whereas pretrained robot representations [31, 48, 55, 72, 77, 95, 97] are compared by frozen-feature imitation, chiefly in CortexBench [51] on MetaWorld [99] and Adroit [73], with further studies varying learner, data and test conditions [11, 14, 16, 23, 28, 60, 76, 78, 83]. We learn policies on OGBench [61] and CortexBench with paired 2D/3D data and compare them with published representations and 2D JEPAs. 3D world models. Most point-cloud JEPAs pretrain encoders without actions [27, 36, 75, 115] or forecast LiDAR occupancy [112] instead of driving planner. Other 3D world models forecast explicit particles [41, 90], points [29, 30, 65, 105], Gaussians [47], depth-augmented video [107], structured latents [42] or occupancy [109], and 3DPWM [65] and PointWorld [30] plan with such forecasts on real arms rather than in latent space. Such explicit forecasts make every prediction visible at the cost of generating each element of the next scene, whereas JEPA world models predict in latent space and have so far left the imagined scene unseen. On the policy side, point-cloud encoders range from PointNet [66, 67] to Point Transformer V3 [93] and Sonata [94], 3D policies condition diffusion heads on such encoders [32, 102, 103], and controlled studies favor point clouds and 3D-aware encoders over 2D inputs [21, 25, 43, 68, 113, 114], but such policies lack world model. Decoders on frozen features map self-supervised representations [10, 108] and the predicted latents of JEPA world models [50, 110] to images, and recent work lifts video world-model rollouts into 3D through generated pixels [33, 87]. Feed-forward networks regress dense point maps from images [37, 85, 86], PAGE-4D [111] extends VGGT to dynamic scenes, and point-set decoders generate or complete clouds [1, 19, 98, 100, 101]. Closest to ours, Oberweger et al. [58] find LeWM on idealized raycast point clouds statistically on par with its pixel version on its own benchmarks. JEPA4R instead reads colored point clouds from one fixed depth camera. Its policy head acts on the frozen latents of world model that can also imagine the scene, and decoder adapted from PAGE-4D turns these latents directly into point clouds. Sim-to-real with 3D observations. Depth and point-cloud observations narrow the gap between simulation and reality: policies trained on them in simulation transfer to real hands and arms [12, 46, 69], point-cloud policies run on real arms and humanoids [102, 103], and point-cloud models resist changes in appearance and viewpoint [64, 102]. Simulators are also matched to the deployment scene. RialTo [82] scans digital twin and robustifies point-cloud policies in it, ACDC [13] generates digital cousins from one image for zero-shot transfer, and Gaussian splatting renders photorealistic RGB for sim-to-real [40, 70]. World models are either learned directly on physical robots [92] or trained in simulation and transferred to legged robots [35, 38] and arms [65, 89]. Among JEPA world models, V-JEPA 2-AC [4] plans on real arms with predictor trained on real robot video, whereas DINO-WM [110] and LeWM [50] are evaluated in simulation. JEPA4R is point-cloud JEPA world model trained in twin of its deployment arm. 3. Ablation Study Decoder backbone. We replace PAGE-4D in the decoder with other feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, keep the set generator, the affine map, the training data and both training stages unchanged, and evaluate again on OGBench Cube (Tab. 4a). PAGE-4D and VGGT give the same per-frame error (0.79 cm), and Depth Anything 3 reaches 0.75 cm. The gap stays as small on imagined rollouts: at environment step 200, PAGE-4D reaches 0.89 cm, VGGT 0.88 cm and Depth Anything 3 0.85 cm. Although PAGE-4D extends VGGT to dynamic scenes, the two decode rollouts equally well. Across the three backbones, each error varies by at most 0.11 cm, so the geometry in the frozen latents does not depend on one particular decoder. Point-cloud encoder. We replace JEPA4Rs PointNet with other point-cloud encoders of the same parameter count, keep the rest of the world model, the training data and the policy head unchanged, and compare on OGBench Scene (Tab. 4b). PointNet reaches the highest success (64.8), so we keep it as JEPA4Rs default encoder. Temporal window. By default, the world model reads three context frames spaced five environment steps apart. We change the number of context frames to two and four, with the policy head unchanged, and compare on OGBench Scene (Tab. 4c). With two frames, success is 63.2, and from three frames on it no longer changes (64.8 with three and with four), so the default of three frames is enough. Training hyperparameters. JEPA4R trains with learning rate of 5105 and batch size of 128. We halve and double the learning rate to 2.5105 and 104, and set the batch size to 64 and 256 while keeping the learning rate and the number of epochs, on OGBench Scene (Tab. 4d). JEPA4R stays between 57.6 and 68.5 in every setting. Changing the learning rate costs at most 2.9 points, whereas the batch size matters more, with 57.6 at 64 and 68.5 at 256. 5.6. Real World Evaluation Robot Setup. We deploy JEPA4R on RealMan RM75-B arm to verify that the world model and policy heads trained only in its digital twin run on real hardware. With an Inspire EG2-4C2 parallel gripper, the arm picks up objects and pushes cubes; with an OYMotion AP001 dexterous hand, it pulls objects out of holder. At every step, JEPA4R encodes the point cloud from single depth camera, and the policy head outputs the next action. Results. JEPA4R completes all three tasks on the real arm. Fig. 8 presents one execution per task, with key frames at Real RM75-B arm p : p h : p G p : H Figure 8. Real-robot deployment of JEPA4R on RealMan RM75-B arm. Key frames of one execution per task at successive time steps, with the camera view above and the point cloud below: picking and pushing with parallel gripper, and picking with dexterous hand. successive time steps. 6. Limitation and Future Work This paper focuses on JEPA world models and policy learning from single-camera point clouds. general world model shared across scenes and robots relies on large-scale, diverse 3D robot data, which remains scarce and is beyond the scope of this paper. How to collect high-quality data for JEPA world models, and whether general recipe exists, remain open questions and are the focus of our next steps. 7. Conclusion Most JEPA world models have seen scenes in 2D, been judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning and hidden what they imagine. JEPA4R predicts, plans and acts in the latent space of single-depth-camera point clouds, and on 3D manipulation tasks it leads the 2D JEPAs by large margin. It ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0% success, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Its decoder turns every imagined rollout into 4D point clouds, with mean point error within 1.1 cm of the observed points over 200 environment steps. Beyond simulation, JEPA4R completes closed-loop deployment on real robot arm with both gripper and dexterous hand, after training only in digital twin. Because manipulation hinges on metric 3D geometry, these results suggest that 3D observations may become the default input of embodied JEPA world models. We hope JEPA4R brings these models closer to robots that plan in 4D point space and check what they imagine before they act. 8. LLM Usage Statement We used large language models (LLMs) as follows. sections.content: S1. Planning under LeWMs setting Following LeWM [50], we also evaluate both world models by goal-reaching planning. Planning encodes the current observation and goal og, unrolls gϕ over = 5 action blocks, and solves t:t+H1 = arg min at:t+H1 (cid:13) (cid:13)ˆzt+H zg (cid:13) 2 2, (cid:13) (S1) with goal latent zg = fθ(og). The cross-entropy method (CEM) [15] samples 300 action sequences, refits Gaussian to the 30 best and repeats 10 times; the robot executes the plan and replans. Equation (S1) thus selects the actions whose imagined outcome ends closest to the goal. For JEPA4R, goal point cloud Pg gives zg = fθ(Pg), and CEM minimizes Eq. (S1) unchanged, since it acts only on latents. We run LeWMs goal-reaching planning on OGBench Cube, with the original UR5e and with the RM75-B twin, which replaces the UR5e. As in LeWM, CEM starts from dataset state and has 50 steps to reach the observation 25 environment steps later. Success requires the cube within 4 cm of its goal (50 starts). Random actions from the same starts give the random-policy floor. Scores are means over the 10 epoch checkpoints. JEPA4R performs on par with LeWM (Tab. S1): their gaps stay within the variation of 50-start estimates on one task, about 6 points. On OGBench Cube, our LeWM run, averaged over its checkpoints, is close to the released checkpoint (69.4 vs. 7274 on our starts). S2. Experimental settings S2.1. Paired data Each world-model dataset is collected in simulation and rendered by one fixed camera into paired images and point clouds that match row by row (Sec. 4.1). On Cube, episodes mix low-noise expert, high-noise expert, expert-then-random and random control in proportions 0.2, 0.4, 0.2 and 0.2; Puzzle follows the noisy recipe of OGBench [61]; on Scene, MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate, they mix noisy expert control, expert control interrupted by random actions, and random actions in proportions 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. Cube has 10,000 episodes per setting, of 200, 500, 1,000 and 600 steps for one to four cubes; Puzzle follows OGBenchs official scale, with 1,000 episodes on 3 3 and 4 4 and 3,000 on 4 5, of 1,001 steps each; Scene, MetaWorld (per task) and Adroit Relocate have 10,000 episodes of 200 steps. World models JEPA4R and the LeWM baseline are identical except for the encoder: PointNet on point clouds for the former and ViT-tiny/14 on images for the latter. Both are trained with Eq. (1) for 10 epochs (AdamW, learning rate 5105, batch size 128), one pair per dataset. S2.3. Policy learning and evaluation Every encoder is frozen, and every benchmark reports success rate. Cube uses GCIQL [61] and Puzzle uses decoupled Q-chunking (DQC) [39], both offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning on OGBenchs official play data for 106 steps: besides the latent, the input carries the robot state on Cube and the button lights on Puzzle, the goal gives the target state of the objects or the lights, and evaluation runs 50 episodes on each of the five official tasks, with Puzzle reporting the best of its ten evaluations during training. MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate use the official imitation protocol of CortexBench [51], and Scene reuses the same code on its five evaluation tasks: behavior cloning for 100 epochs on 25 demonstrations per task (100 on Relocate), scoring the best of 20 evaluations. S2.4. Baselines PLDM [79] and LeJEPA [5] are trained on our image data for 10 epochs with their own recipes; VISReg [91] and VJEPA 2.1 [54] use the authors released weights and are evaluated by us. All four encoders are frozen, with the same policy learning and evaluation as JEPA4R. PLDM and LeJEPA use ViT-tiny/14 and VISReg and V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-B/16; on Cube, PLDM uses an Impala encoder and V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L/16. Outlook. The approach is promising in several directions. On the 3D representation that JEPA4R learns, policy can be trained from little data and deployed on the real arm, which suits robotic settings where real data are expensive and hard to collect at scale; the world model and the policy head, trained only in digital twin, run zero-shot on the real arm, so embodied world models can be trained mainly in digital twins rather than on large amounts of real robot video. The JEPA recipe carries over to point clouds with the predictor and the objective unchanged, the same upgrade applies to other JEPA world models, and 3D observations may become the default input of embodied JEPA world models. The decoder shows that, while training stays free of reconstruction, frozen latents and entire imagined rollouts can still be decoded into metrically accurate 4D point clouds, so robot can check the expected outcome of an action sequence before executing it; building on this, planning can move from approaching goal latent to operating in 4D point space, with goals given directly as point clouds and every imagined step checkable in metric space. Finally, combining paired 2D/3D data with policy learning offers way to compare world-model representations beyond shorthorizon planning. S3. Visualizations We show one successful episode of JEPA4R for every simulated task (Figs. S1 to S4), more decoded imagination on OGBench Cube-Single (Figs. S5 and S6) and all eight realrobot executions (Figs. S7 and S8). In every figure, frames run from left to right; the camera view is shown for reference, and JEPA4R receives the point cloud below it. Simulated tasks. On OGBench, UR5e arm picks and places one, two or three cubes into goal arrangement on Cube; on the Scene task shown, it presses button to unlock drawer, opens the drawer, puts the cube inside and closes it; on Puzzle, it presses buttons that toggle the neighboring lights until the board matches the goal pattern. On MetaWorld, Sawyer arm puts ring onto peg (Assembly), moves cube from one bin to the other (Bin-pick), presses button from the top (Button), opens drawer (Drawer) and drives nail with hammer (Hammer). On Adroit Relocate, dexterous hand picks up ball and moves it to target. Each episode runs from the start to the first success. Decoded imagination. As in Fig. 7, the world model receives three context frames and then predicts from the recorded actions alone, and the decoder turns every imagined latent into point cloud. In each of the six test episodes, the cube starts on the table, is lifted and is put down again. Real robot. All eight executions run zero-shot on the RealMan RM75-B arm with policies trained only in its digital twin. With the Inspire EG2-4C2 parallel gripper, the arm pushes cubes together and picks up carrot, cucumber and chili; with the OYMotion AP001 dexterous hand, it pulls bar, bottle, carrot and banana out of slotted holder. S4. Discussion What the results mean. The results argue for three changes to the JEPA route. First, 3D-native input: an image entangles metric geometry with appearance and perspective, so pixel model must infer depth, whereas point cloud records visible surfaces at their metric positions; the decoding results in Sec. 5.4 also show that frozen point-cloud latents retain this metric geometry, from which the policy head can read where the objects and the gripper are in space. Second, evaluation through the policies robots learn, rather than through short-horizon goal reaching alone: latents that plan well can transfer poorly to policy learning [45], so evaluating by planning alone does not show whether representation serves policy learning. Third, decoded latents as standard diagnostic: frozen latents decode back to point clouds, so imagined futures can be compared directly with observations.
